c.text: 28 MARCH 2011
NASA's Swift satellite suddenly detected an extremely bright flash in the sky
It came from the direction of the constellation Draco, and it carried gamma rays
At first astronomers thought it was a normal gamma-ray burst...
...the last blast of a dying star, over in seconds or minutes
But this time, that's not what happened
The flash didn't stop
First for hours, then days, and finally weeks
X-rays kept pouring in from that same patch of sky
The place was about 3.8 billion light-years from Earth
And whatever was happening there shone brighter than 100 billion Suns
Astronomer Joshua Bloom and his team pointed Hubble and Chandra in that direction
The flash was coming from the very centre of a quiet galaxy
A big black hole sat there, perhaps twice as massive as the one in our galaxy
It had been quiet for a long time
Then a star like our Sun wandered very close to it

c.text: A black hole can break a star without swallowing it whole
Astrophysicist Jack Hills explained this idea in 1975
Around every massive black hole is an invisible boundary called the tidal radius
Inside it, gravity behaves differently
The side of the star nearest the black hole is pulled much harder than the far side
That difference stretches the star
For a person, the pull on the feet would be far stronger than on the head
And the whole body would slowly be pulled into a thin line
In 1988, Stephen Hawking gave it a fun name in his book A Brief History of Time
SPAGHETTIFICATION
In 2011, exactly this happened to that star
The star's own gravity lost to the black hole's pull
First its round shape became a drop, then a long stream

c.text: And within hours, it was completely shredded
But the black hole didn't swallow the whole star at once
About half the star's gas flew back into space at thousands of kilometres per second
The other half began to circle the black hole
It spun so fast that friction heated it to millions of degrees
That made a glowing disk of light, called an accretion disk
Meanwhile, its magnetic fields launched some gas in two straight beams far into space
These beams are called jets
They moved at about 99.5 percent of the speed of light
And one of those jets was pointed straight at Earth
That's why the event looked so bright to us
Torn-apart stars had been seen before...
...but this was the first time the jet from one pointed straight at Earth

c.text: But the 2011 black hole was nothing next to the universe's biggest predators
And some black holes still puzzle scientists
OCTOBER 2018
In October 2018, a telescope survey spotted another unusual flash, about 665 million light-years away
Another black hole had torn a star apart
Within months the flash faded, and scientists moved on
In June 2021, about three years later, Harvard astronomer Yvette Cendes and her team looked at that spot again
They used the Very Large Array radio telescope in New Mexico
What they saw was a surprise
The black hole had become active again
Without eating another star, it was hurling gas into space at half the speed of light
Cendes explained it with a funny example
Like someone who suddenly burps years after a meal
Scientists jokingly named it...
JETTY McJETFACE
No one knows for sure where the black hole kept that gas all those years

c.text: Now, one of the biggest predators in the universe
Its name is TON 618
In 1957, at Mexico's Tonantzintla Observatory...
...two astronomers were listing objects that glow blue
At number 618 was a faint blue object
Nobody knew what it really was
In 1970, radio observations in Bologna, Italy showed it was not a star but a quasar
A quasar is where a giant black hole keeps feeding on gas...
...releasing so much energy it can outshine an entire galaxy
In 2004, astronomers estimated its mass
By some estimates, about 66 billion times the mass of our Sun
It is called an ultramassive black hole
Its event horizon, the boundary from which not even light returns, spans about 2,600 astronomical units
One astronomical unit is the distance between Earth and the Sun
Neptune is only 30 astronomical units from the Sun

c.at: अगर टॉन छह सौ अठारह को
c.text: Put TON 618 where our Sun is, and the whole solar system would fit inside it
Light would take about two weeks to cross it from one edge to the other
The gas around it shines like 140 trillion Suns
But giant black holes like this have one strange habit...
...they usually don't tear stars apart
The heavier a black hole, the faster its event horizon grows, but its tidal radius doesn't keep up
Above about 100 million solar masses, the tidal radius falls inside the event horizon
So a star like our Sun reaching TON 618 wouldn't stretch and break
No spectacular flash
TON 618 would swallow it whole, in complete silence

c.text: TON 618 is more than 10 billion light-years from Earth
But a massive black hole sits at the centre of our own galaxy too
In 1974, American astronomers Bruce Balick and Robert Brown used the radio telescopes at Green Bank
They detected a powerful radio signal at the centre of the Milky Way
About 26,000 light-years from Earth
SAGITTARIUS A*
For thirty years, teams led by Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel tracked the stars circling that spot
With the Keck and Very Large Telescope observatories
One of them is a star called S2
When it passes closest to that invisible object, it reaches about 7,700 kilometres per second
About 2.5 percent of the speed of light
Their motion confirmed a black hole of about 4 million Suns
For this discovery, Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics
And in May 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope showed the world the first image of Sagittarius A*
Today this black hole is fairly quiet...
...there isn't much gas around it to eat
But it wasn't always this way

c.text: JUNE 2023
Astronomer Frederic Marin and his team at Strasbourg Observatory analysed data from NASA's IXPE satellite
Gas clouds around Sagittarius A* were glowing in X-rays
When they measured the light's polarization, they found something surprising
The light wasn't the clouds' own
It was an old flash from Sagittarius A*...
...reflected by the clouds, and only now reaching Earth
About 200 years ago, this black hole became active for a while
Perhaps it consumed a gas cloud nearby
For about a year it was at least a million times brighter than today
Then it went quiet again
In our galaxy this happens once every 10,000 to 100,000 years...
...a wandering star comes too close to this black hole and is torn apart

c.text: But this quiet black hole may show its true face when our galaxy meets a huge cosmic collision
Our neighbour, the Andromeda galaxy, is approaching at about 110 kilometres per second
Scientists used to think a collision in about 4 billion years was almost certain
But a 2025 study puts the chance of a collision in the next 10 billion years at about 50 percent
If it happens, billions of stars and huge gas clouds could fall toward the centre
Sagittarius A* and Andromeda's black hole could circle each other and finally merge
Then our sleeping black hole might fully wake up
Star after star could be torn apart, and a powerful quasar could ignite at the centre
What Swift saw in 2011 wasn't just a story about a distant galaxy
It may have been a glimpse of our own galaxy's future
The stars look calm in the sky
But behind that darkness, a game of gravity never stops, one we still don't fully understand
And the universe's hunters are simply waiting for the next wandering star
